assertions.statement: The convolutional neural network (CNN) method learns the entire processing pipeline directly from raw sensor data to generate steering commands from a single front-facing camera image.
Approaches like ChauffeurNet employ recurrent neural networks (RNNs) that utilize mid-level input representations to predict driving trajectories.
This facilitates training on both real and simulated data.
This enables closed-loop simulation testing before deployment.
Early systems such as ALVINN demonstrated the feasibility of end-to-end neural network steering using relatively small fully-connected networks and limited data.
Modern CNN-based systems leverage greater computational power and extensive datasets to improve robustness and vehicle independence.
There is a noted contradiction regarding the reliability of end-to-end trained networks.
ALVINN showed successful steering on public roads.
Other systems like DAVE were not reliable enough to replace modular approaches.
This highlights challenges in generalizability.
Pure imitation learning, even with large datasets and mid-level representations, faces significant limitations.
These limitations are due to error accumulation and distribution shift during closed-loop operation.
These issues manifest as failures such as getting stuck or collisions despite viable passing options.
This indicates that pure imitation learning alone may be insufficient for reliable autonomous driving.
Some advancements have been made using purely offline data without reinforcement learning.
This suggests ongoing progress in this area.
Mid-level representations combined with recurrent architectures enhance model training and simulation by allowing iterative prediction refinement.
They allow integration of perception modules.
This supports more effective closed-loop testing and deployment.
The CARLA simulator serves as a comprehensive open-source platform for autonomous urban driving research.
It provides detailed urban layouts, vehicles, pedestrians, and flexible sensor suite specifications.
CARLA supports development, training, prototyping, and validation of autonomous driving models.
This includes classic modular pipelines, end-to-end imitation learning, and reinforcement learning approaches.
CARLA enables evaluation in controlled scenarios with specific metrics.
It offers measurements of agent state and traffic rule compliance.
These measurements are critical for training and assessment.
Comparisons between simulation-based platforms like CARLA and real-world data-driven methods such as DARPA's DAVE project illustrate differing approaches in autonomous driving research.
Significant gaps remain, particularly in addressing error accumulation and distribution shift in closed-loop imitation learning.
Current methods do not adequately mitigate these challenges.
This underscores the need for novel strategies to improve robustness and reliability in autonomous driving systems.
